description: From rotten boroughs to equal franchise — how Britain's electorate expanded between 1832 and 1928.
content_html:
The Unreformed Electoral System

By the early nineteenth century, Britain’s system of parliamentary representation had not kept pace with population change. Many rotten boroughs returned MPs despite having almost no voters: Old Sarum in Wiltshire had seven voters and two MPs; Manchester, a growing industrial city with over 100,000 people, had none. The right to vote varied chaotically between constituencies — in some a man needed a forty-shilling freehold, in others any male householder could vote. Most working-class men and all women were excluded entirely.

The economic and social pressures of industrialisation made reform increasingly urgent. A rapidly growing urban working class had no representation. The fear of popular unrest — the French Revolution was a recent memory — made many MPs nervous about ignoring pressure for change.

Key Fact

A rotten borough was a constituency with almost no voters, often controlled by a single landlord. Old Sarum (Wiltshire) had seven voters and returned two MPs. Meanwhile Manchester, with over 100,000 inhabitants, had no MP at all. This made the pre-1832 Parliament deeply unrepresentative.

The Great Reform Act 1832

The Great Reform Act of 1832 was passed by Lord Grey’s Whig government after sustained popular pressure. It abolished the worst rotten boroughs, gave seats to the new industrial towns (Manchester, Birmingham, Leeds, Sheffield), and extended the vote in boroughs to men who occupied property worth at least £10 a year.

The Act nearly doubled the electorate from around 400,000 to around 650,000. But it remained a very partial reform: it said nothing about the secret ballot (votes were still cast publicly, leaving tenants vulnerable to landlord pressure), and it did not enfranchise working-class men or women. It was a reform that preserved property ownership as the qualification for political participation.

The Second Reform Act of 1867 was a much bolder step. Passed by Benjamin Disraeli’s Conservative government, it extended the vote in boroughs to male householders and some lodgers, adding around a million new voters and giving the vote to many urban working-class men for the first time. Disraeli calculated that the newly enfranchised working class would be grateful and vote Conservative — a calculation that proved partly wrong.

William Gladstone’s Third Reform Act of 1884 extended the same franchise to rural areas, adding another 1.5 million voters. The Redistribution Act of 1885 followed, redrawing constituency boundaries to reflect population. By 1885, roughly two-thirds of adult men could vote — but no women, and not the poorest urban men.

Suffragists and Suffragettes

The campaign for women’s suffrage developed two distinct wings, which students must not confuse. The suffragists — the NUWSS led by Millicent Fawcett — pursued women’s votes through constitutional means: petitions, meetings, lobbying MPs, and peaceful demonstration. Fawcett had been campaigning since the 1860s and believed patient constitutional pressure would succeed.

The suffragettes — the WSPU founded in 1903 by Emmeline Pankhurst — took direct action: smashing windows, chaining themselves to railings, arson attacks on post boxes and empty buildings, and hunger strikes in prison. Emily Davison was killed at Epsom on 4 June 1913 when she ran onto the racecourse during the Derby. Emmeline’s daughters Christabel and Sylvia both played prominent roles, though they later disagreed: Christabel continued the militant campaign, while Sylvia worked with the labour movement and opposed the First World War.

Key Fact

Suffragists (NUWSS, led by Millicent Fawcett) used constitutional means — petitions and lobbying. Suffragettes (WSPU, led by Emmeline Pankhurst) used militant direct action — arson, window-smashing and hunger strikes. Examiners penalise using these terms interchangeably.

The Representation of the People Act 1918 gave the vote to all men over 21 and to women over 30 who met a property qualification. Around 8.4 million women gained the vote. The age and property bar on women was clearly discriminatory, but it prevented women — who outnumbered men after the war’s casualties — from forming a majority of the electorate.

Why 1918? Historians point to several factors: women’s vital contributions to the war effort (munitions, nursing, transport) made it impossible to deny their civic participation; the WSPU had suspended militancy during the war and thrown itself into patriotic service; the Representation of the People Act was also driven by the need to give the vote to millions of servicemen who had lost it by moving away from their homes. Full equal franchise came in 1928, when the Equal Franchise Act lowered the voting age for women to 21, equalising the franchise.
exam_tip_html: Examiner reports for this unit specifically flag the error of using “suffragette” as a generic term for all women who campaigned for the vote. The WSPU (Emmeline Pankhurst) and the NUWSS (Millicent Fawcett) were distinct organisations with different tactics and different views on the effectiveness of militancy. In an “Explain Why” question on why women won the vote in 1918, a top-band answer will weigh both organisations’ contributions alongside the impact of the First World War — and should not present the WSPU as the sole or even primary cause.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Great Reform Act (1832) abolished rotten boroughs and extended the vote to the middle class, but left working-class men and all women unrepresented.
  • The Second (1867) and Third (1884) Reform Acts progressively extended male suffrage to urban and then rural workers — by 1885 roughly two-thirds of adult men could vote.
  • Women over 30 with a property qualification won the vote in 1918; equal franchise for all women over 21 came in 1928, driven by both the constitutional NUWSS campaign and the militant WSPU, alongside the impact of the First World War.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Great Reform Act (1832).
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Mastering: identifies a specific reform (e.g. it abolished rotten boroughs) AND develops it with accurate detail (e.g. Old Sarum had seven voters and two MPs; the Act removed such constituencies and redistributed their seats to new industrial towns like Manchester and Birmingham). Secure: valid feature with limited development. Developing: vague reference to increasing the electorate. Emerging: irrelevant or no attempt.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the campaign for women's suffrage.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per feature. Mastering: two accurate features clearly distinguishing between suffragist and suffragette tactics (e.g. the NUWSS under Millicent Fawcett used constitutional lobbying and peaceful petition — a non-violent strategy of persuading Parliament; the WSPU under Emmeline Pankhurst used militant direct action including arson attacks and hunger strikes — designed to make the political cost of continued refusal too high). Secure: both features with some development. Developing: one feature well described, one vague or confusing the two organisations. Emerging: vague reference to women protesting.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Great Reform Act (1832) was a limited reform.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: two or more reasons with specific evidence (it extended the vote only to men with property worth £10/year in boroughs — leaving most working-class men unrepresented; there was still no secret ballot, leaving tenants vulnerable to landlord pressure; no women were enfranchised; the electorate grew from about 400,000 to 650,000 — still a tiny fraction of the population; the principle of property as the franchise qualification was retained, not abolished). Secure: two reasons with some specific detail. Developing: one developed reason or two undeveloped. Emerging: describes the Act accurately but does not explain why it was limited.

practice_questions.text: Explain why women gained the vote in 1918 rather than earlier.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: explains two or more factors that made 1918 the moment (women's war work in munitions, nursing and transport made their civic contribution impossible to ignore; the WSPU suspended militancy during the war, making a hostile government response less defensible; the 1918 Act was partly driven by the need to enfranchise servicemen — women's inclusion became politically viable at the same moment; constitutional campaigning by the NUWSS had built sustained parliamentary support over decades). Considers why earlier attempts failed. Secure: two factors with some specific evidence. Developing: one factor developed or two undeveloped. Emerging: simply states that women worked in the war without explaining the political connection.

practice_questions.text: How far did the Reform Acts of 1832-1884 represent a genuine transfer of power to the people? [You may consider: rotten boroughs; the extension of the franchise; women's suffrage; and any other relevant factors.]
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: sustained argument acknowledging both real change (abolition of rotten boroughs; towns represented for first time; working-class urban then rural men enfranchised; electorate grew from 400,000 to c.5 million 1832-1885) and significant continuity (property qualification retained; no secret ballot until 1872; no women enfranchised; most working-class men still excluded in 1867; 'transfer of power to the people' only complete in 1928 with equal franchise). Overall judgement required. Secure: argues both sides with relevant evidence; some imbalance. Developing: describes reforms accurately but does not weigh the extent of power transfer. Emerging: narrative of reform acts without addressing the question.

practice_questions.text: Outline the main differences between the suffragist and suffragette campaigns for votes for women.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: three or more specific comparative points (NUWSS vs WSPU; Fawcett vs Pankhurst; constitutional lobbying vs militant direct action; petitions and meetings vs arson and hunger strikes; NUWSS supported the war effort throughout; WSPU suspended militancy 1914; Sylvia Pankhurst split from WSPU over the war). Secure: two or three accurate comparative points. Developing: one point of comparison, or describes one organisation only. Emerging: vague reference to different tactics.

knowledge_checks.q: Which Act (1832) abolished rotten boroughs and extended the vote to middle-class property owners for the first time?
The NUWSS, which used constitutional means to campaign for women's votes, was led by whom?
The Equal Franchise Act of _____ gave all women over 21 the right to vote, equalising the franchise between men and women.
The Second Reform Act of 1867 extended the vote in boroughs to male _____ and some lodgers, adding around a million new voters.
Match each Reform Act to the government that passed it:

flashcard_questions.q: What was a rotten borough? Give one example.
flashcard_questions.a: A constituency with almost no voters — Old Sarum had seven voters and two MPs while Manchester (100,000+ people) had none.

flashcard_questions.q: What did the Great Reform Act (1832) do?
flashcard_questions.a: Abolished rotten boroughs, gave seats to new industrial towns, extended the vote to men with property worth £10 a year.

flashcard_questions.q: Which year did the Second Reform Act pass and who led the government?
What did the Third Reform Act (1884) achieve?
flashcard_questions.a: Extended the same franchise as the 1867 Act to rural labourers, adding around 1.5 million new voters.

flashcard_questions.q: What was the WSPU and who founded it?
flashcard_questions.a: Women's Social and Political Union, founded 1903 by Emmeline Pankhurst — used militant tactics including arson and hunger strikes.

flashcard_questions.q: What was the NUWSS and who led it?
flashcard_questions.a: National Union of Women's Suffrage Societies, led by Millicent Fawcett — used constitutional lobbying and peaceful protest.

flashcard_questions.q: What did the Representation of the People Act 1918 establish?
flashcard_questions.a: The vote for all men over 21 and women over 30 with a property qualification — around 8.4 million women enfranchised.

flashcard_questions.q: When was the Equal Franchise Act and what did it do?
flashcard_questions.a: 1928 — gave all women over 21 the vote, finally equalising the franchise.

flashcard_questions.q: Who was Emily Davison and what happened to her?
flashcard_questions.a: A WSPU suffragette killed at the Epsom Derby on 4 June 1913 when she ran onto the racecourse.

glossary_terms.definition: Constituencies with very few voters, often controlled by a single landowner — able to return an MP despite having almost no resident electorate.
The 1832 Act of Parliament that abolished rotten boroughs, redistributed seats to the new industrial towns, and extended the vote to middle-class property owners.
The 1867 Act, passed by Benjamin Disraeli's Conservative government, which extended the vote in towns to male householders and lodgers, roughly doubling the urban electorate.
The 1884 Act, passed by Gladstone's Liberal government, which extended the same voting rights given to urban workers in 1867 to rural labourers.
The National Union of Women's Suffrage Societies (NUWSS), founded 1897, led by Millicent Fawcett, which pursued women's votes through constitutional lobbying and non-violent campaigning.
The Women's Social and Political Union (WSPU), founded 1903 by Emmeline Pankhurst, which used militant tactics including arson, window-smashing and hunger strikes to demand votes for women.
The 1918 Act that gave the vote to all men over 21 and to women over 30 who met a property qualification — the largest single extension of the franchise in British history.
The 1928 Act that gave the vote to all women over 21, equalising the franchise between men and women.
